2009–2022 drafts / The first four seasons

NBA Draft Success

What happens in the first four seasons?

Page sections
ExplorerHow the model worksLimitationsDefinitionsSources and code

Earlier picks tend to deliver more wins. Draft position is less tied to impact per possession.

Same-population check: among the same 735 complete rated participants, pick–WAR rank correlation is -0.45, compared with -0.13 for pick–LEBRON. All 828 complete WAR outcomes give -0.52. How the model works

We evaluate draft classes retrospectively. The 2019 class’s four-season window ends in 2022–23, so these outcomes were unavailable on 2020 draft night.

Method
Scope and all-pick audit data

What the difference means

For 2009–2022 selections, earlier slots tended to produce more four-season WAR. Draft position had a weaker relationship with LEBRON among rated NBA participants. That rate comparison excludes players without a measured rate.

For a team, this separates two questions: how much NBA value a slot produced, including players who never appeared, and how effective its measured NBA participants were while playing. Neither quantity is pure talent.

At pick 41, the four-year WAR mean is 3.81, while the four-season median is 0.47 WAR across 14 complete selections. The average and the typical middle outcome tell different stories.

Why the pick-41 average is not a typical outcome

Nikola Jokić, drafted 2014 at pick 41, produced 26.09 WAR and a 4.06 LEBRON rate in 6214 NBA minutes over the 2014-15 through 2017-18 window. He played in 3 of those four seasons; the waiting season still counts. Highest observed four-season WAR among the 14 pick-41 outcomes; an upside example, not a typical outcome or contract surplus. Includes a draft-to-debut waiting season.

How the model works

Formulas

We hold out one development class at a time within 2009–2019. We select the simplest model within one standard error of the lowest mean class RMSE, test on 2020–2022, then refit for display. The four-year window starts at selection; the 2020 draft starts in 2020–21.

Final rate equation: LEBRON = -0.896958. Final WAR equation: WAR = 14.695272 + (-3.455910 × ln(pick)). The logarithm lets the fitted decline differ between early and later slots.

These retrospective fits describe the sample. They cannot predict an individual outcome or establish an effect of draft position.

We resample whole draft classes for 95% percentile intervals. Curve intervals describe uncertainty about means while holding the selected model fixed.

Validation and research

Where does a pick depart from the fitted trend?

We compare mean WAR with the fitted curve across 60 slots. Simultaneous bands account for scanning those slots together, conditional on the chosen model.

Pick 56 averages 0.11 WAR versus a fitted 0.78: residual −0.68, with a simultaneous 95% band of −1.26 to −0.09. Removing each slot’s highest-WAR player and refitting shrinks the residual to −0.14. Another eligible curve can change its sign.

Pick 56: period and exceptional-player checks

Against the main curve, pick 56’s residual is −0.66 in 2009–2015 and −0.69 in 2016–2022. These period checks remain conditional on that curve and cannot establish a lasting slot effect.

Limitations

Limitations

  • WAR includes production for any NBA team, including teams other than the drafting club.
  • Four seasons cover early contribution. Age, delayed debuts, injuries and opportunity affect outcomes.
  • LEBRON estimates context-sensitive impact rather than isolated talent or scouting quality.
  • Up to 14 classes support each slot. Variable outcomes and overlapping mean intervals limit precise rankings.
  • Lockout and COVID seasons offer different numbers of games.
  • We use one retrospective rating snapshot, without verifying draft-date availability.
  • Unresolved positive-minute metrics remain excluded.
  • Rate comparisons select for NBA participation and measurement.
  • Held-out error comes from three test classes; the final fit includes them after evaluation.
  • Curve intervals omit provider-rating and model-selection uncertainty.
  • Anomaly scans remain exploratory despite simultaneous bands and sensitivity checks.
  • Trade references pair a dated cap-hit ceiling with prior-season WAR. They cannot value future control or unequal contract lengths.

Definitions

Definitions

LEBRON
Estimated impact per 100 possessions, with zero at league average. We weight each player’s window by provider possessions, then weight players equally within picks. No minutes means no rate.
Accumulated WAR
Provider WAR summed across the four post-draft regular seasons. Negative values remain; confirmed absent seasons contribute zero.
Four-season window
The four seasons after selection, including any wait before debut. The 2020 draft starts in 2020–21.
Association
A relationship between draft position and outcomes, without a causal interpretation.
Historical player equivalent
An illustration from observed four-season outcomes. The optional joint-profile match uses WAR, minutes and rate standardized by cohort SD. A warning flags a WAR mismatch larger than the slot’s interquartile range; this is a display heuristic.
Confidence interval
Uncertainty about a mean under class resampling. Individual outcomes can fall far outside it.
Held-out draft classes
Classes excluded during fitting. Selection uses 2009–2019; testing uses 2020–2022.
Trade reference
Divide fitted four-season WAR by four, then match observed 2025–26 WAR within the signed-player pool under each 2026–27 cap ceiling. Both sides use annual units; this is a historical production reference.
Same-slot player example
An actual same-slot draftee nearest the 25th, 50th or 90th WAR percentile. Match on WAR alone; break ties by earlier class. Show actual minutes, rate and signed WAR mismatch. Nonparticipants retain zero WAR and minutes, with no rate.
Rated-player retention
Players rated in years one and four divided by players rated in year one.
Paired player change
Year-four minus year-one LEBRON for the same returning rated players. Selection prevents a causal development interpretation.
Matched adjacent-slot contrast
Later-slot minus earlier-slot outcomes within matched classes. Pointwise intervals lack a correction across neighboring pairs.
Four-season 1,000-minute threshold
At least 1,000 total NBA minutes across the four seasons.
One-season 1,000-minute proxy
At least one post-draft season with 1,000 NBA minutes. This measures exposure, without certifying role or quality.
Delayed debut
First NBA appearance in years two through four. No-debut players remain separate.
Cross-validation (CV)
Hold out one development class, fit on the others, and measure error on that class. Average the class errors.
Root mean squared error (RMSE)
Square prediction errors, average them, then take the square root. RMSE uses outcome units and emphasizes large misses.
Standard error and the one-SE rule
Keep the simplest model within one standard error of the best average CV error. SE = standard deviation of class errors ÷ √number of classes.
R²
Test R² compares error with the development-mean baseline; negative means worse. Final-fit R² measures in-sample fit.
Bootstrap
Resample whole classes with replacement, preserving their players together. Intervals use 2,000 samples and hold model choice fixed.
Natural spline and degrees of freedom
A smooth segmented curve with linear tails. More degrees of freedom permit more curvature.
Percentiles
Positions in observed outcomes. The median is the 50th percentile; the 25th–75th interval contains the middle half.
